summary: Defines a method for negotiating data compression over PPP links. It is on the standards track as a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Two computers on a phone line first agree on whether to squish the data, and how, before they start sending it.

questions: what is ppp compression control protocol
what ppp protocol number does ccp use
subtitle: How the two ends of a PPP link agree on whether to compress data, and which method to use.

tldr.problem: PPP can carry many kinds of traffic, but the two ends need a standard way to agree on a compression method, and a way to recover if compression goes wrong.
tldr.mechanism: CCP reuses the packet exchange and option negotiation of PPP's Link Control Protocol with its own set of options, and adds Reset-Request and Reset-Ack packets so one direction can recover from a decompression failure.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines how to negotiate compression but does not pick an algorithm. It is a Proposed Standard that was later updated by RFC 2153.

today: RFC 1962 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 2153. Its option type values were to be tracked in the "Assigned Numbers" RFC rather than in this document.

sections.title: Why PPP Needs a Compression Protocol
sections.content:
After the two ends of a PPP link have used LCP packets to configure and test the link, optional facilities can be negotiated. Data compression is one of them. Many methods may be negotiated, though typically only one is used in each direction of the link.

A different algorithm may be chosen for each direction, for reasons of speed, cost or memory, or only one direction may be compressed at all.
sections.plainLanguage: Before two friends pass notes written in shorthand, they agree which shorthand to use. They can even use a different one in each direction.

sections.title: CCP Is LCP With a Few Changes
sections.content:
The Compression Control Protocol (CCP) configures, enables and disables compression algorithms at both ends of the link. It also signals a failure of the compression or decompression mechanism in a reliable way.

CCP is exactly the same as the Link Control Protocol with a short list of exceptions. One CCP packet is carried in the PPP Information field, with PPP Protocol field value hex 80FD. For individual link compression across several links to one destination the value is hex 80FB. Besides Codes 1 through 7 (Configure-Request, Configure-Ack, Configure-Nak, Configure-Reject, Terminate-Request, Terminate-Ack and Code-Reject), CCP adds Code 14 (Reset-Request) and Code 15 (Reset-Ack). Other codes should be answered with Code-Rejects.

CCP packets cannot be exchanged until PPP reaches the Network-Layer Protocol phase, and packets that arrive earlier should be silently discarded. Implementations should be prepared to wait for Authentication and Link Quality Determination to finish before timing out, and it is suggested they give up only after user intervention or a configurable amount of time.
sections.plainLanguage: CCP is a copy of the "let us agree on settings" conversation PPP already has, with a different list of things to agree about and two extra messages for "start over".

sections.title: Sending Compressed Datagrams
sections.content:
Compressed packets may be sent only after PPP has reached the Network-Layer Protocol phase and CCP has reached the Opened state. They travel in the PPP Information field with PPP Protocol field hex 00FD (compressed datagram). The protocol field says the frame is compressed, but not which algorithm was used. Only one primary algorithm is in use in each direction at a time, and it is negotiated before the first compressed frame.

With several PPP links to one destination, data can be compressed before it is split across the links, or each link can be treated as its own connection. In the second case the PPP Protocol field MUST be hex 00FB (individual link compressed datagram).

A compressed packet may be no longer than the maximum Information field of a PPP packet. If compression made a datagram larger, it may be sent uncompressed in standard form, or split into several datagrams if the algorithm supports that.

Each algorithm must supply a way to tell whether it is passing data reliably, or it must require a reliable transport such as LAPB. Vendors are strongly encouraged to validate compressed data or recognize compressor and decompressor pairs that are out of sync.
sections.plainLanguage: Squished packets get their own "this is squished" label, but the label does not say which squishing method was used, since both sides already agreed on that.

sections.title: Reset-Request and Reset-Ack
sections.content:
The Reset-Request and Reset-Ack codes let one end report a decompression failure in one direction without disturbing traffic in the other direction. The failure might be found by passing a hash value periodically, by a CRC check on the decompressed data, or by another mechanism. The RFC strongly suggests that every algorithm provide some way to validate decompressed data.

A receiver that detects failure SHOULD send a packet with Code 14 (Reset-Request) and any data it wants in the Data field. It then discards compressed packets it receives and resends the request with the same Identifier until a valid Reset-Ack arrives.

When a Reset-Request arrives, the transmitting compressor is reset to its initial state, for example by clearing a dictionary or resetting hash codes. The peer MUST answer with Code 15 (Reset-Ack), copying the Identifier from the request. When a Reset-Ack arrives, the receiving decompressor is reset as well, and because several Reset-Acks may be in flight it MUST be reset for each Reset-Ack that matches the currently expected identifier.

The Identifier MUST change whenever the Data content changes and whenever a valid reply has been received for a previous request. For retransmissions it MAY stay the same. The Data field is zero or more octets of uninterpreted data, up to the peer's established MRU minus four.
sections.plainLanguage: If one side cannot understand the shorthand any more, it says "stop, start over". The other side clears its notes and says "done", and both begin again from the same page.

sections.title: CCP Configuration Options
sections.content:
CCP uses the Configuration Option format of LCP, with a separate set of option types. Each option names an algorithm that the receiver is willing or able to use to decompress data from the sender, so systems are expected to offer several and settle on one.

The normal LCP negotiation rules apply. An unrecognized option MUST get a Configure-Reject. If all of the sender's algorithms are rejected, no compression is used in that direction. A recognized option with unacceptable values MUST get a Configure-NAK containing only acceptable options, and a new Configure-Request SHOULD then carry only the single preferred option. If no agreement is possible, the link simply runs without compression.

Option 0 is the proprietary compression option. It carries the vendor's IEEE Organization Unique Identifier (OUI), the three most significant octets of an Ethernet physical address, followed by a Subtype and Values that are specific to the vendor. Its length is at least 6. Since the first matching compression is used, known OUI options are recommended to be sent first. The implementation must verify that it can decompress the proprietary algorithm and fully understands the vendor-specific values before accepting.

Other option types, 1 to 254, name publicly defined algorithms, with a length of at least 2. The RFC says no particular technique has arisen as an Internet Standard, and some may carry licensing restrictions. The values 4 through 15 are unassigned and intended for freely available algorithms with no license fees.
sections.plainLanguage: Each side lists the shorthands it can read. They keep going through the lists until they find one both know. If there is none, they just write in plain words.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says only that security issues are not discussed in the memo. It has no security section beyond that one sentence, so any security questions about compression have to be answered elsewhere.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC does not talk about security.
